properties.name: cipherhorizon:pqc:rationale
properties.value: Symmetric block cipher. The best known quantum attack on key search, Grover's algorithm, gives only a quadratic speed-up, so an n-bit key keeps about n/2 bits of quantum security. NIST defines post-quantum security categories 1, 3 and 5 as the cost of key search against AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256, so AES at any key size the standard defines meets at least category 1. This is a statement about the algorithm, not about the key size or mode in use on a given host.

properties.name: cipherhorizon:pqc:basis
properties.value: NIST PQC security categories: 1/3/5 are defined by AES-128/192/256 key search, 2/4 by SHA-256/SHA-384 collision search <https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/post-quantum-cryptography/post-quantum-cryptography-standardization/evaluation-criteria/security-(evaluation-criteria)>

properties.name: cipherhorizon:pqc:rationale
properties.value: Relies on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem in a finite field. Shor's algorithm solves discrete logarithms in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer.

properties.value: Relies on the hardness of the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem. Applies to the Edwards and Montgomery curves used by EdDSA and X25519/X448 as it does to the NIST curves.

properties.name: cipherhorizon:pqc:rationale
properties.value: Relies on the hardness of integer factorization. Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer, so larger keys raise the quantum resources needed only polynomially and give no lasting protection.
